title: The khatm: every letter, every meaning
hook: a Qur'an heard from beginning to end
carry: a khatm honors every letter and every meaning
tomorrow: why does a coffee shop smell like a hadith?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the thirtieth part: the short surahs at the back of the book, kept by heart because you keep returning. Today, the rest of the book, all of it.

Some people finish a whole series in one weekend. Others make one episode last a week and argue about it after. Same show, two ways to love it. Now put a Qur'an on the kitchen table. A grandmother wants it read from beginning to end at home before her granddaughter flies back to college: aunts, cousins, neighbors, each taking a part. Fast, together, finished. And a cousin pushes back: what's the point of racing through Arabic you don't understand? How fast is too fast? Both of them have the tradition on their side.
screen: `ONE WEEKEND, OR ONE A WEEK?` → `A QUR'AN ON THE KITCHEN TABLE.` → `HOW FAST IS TOO FAST?`

segments.voice: First, the case for finishing. Reading the whole Qur'an through is called a khatm, a sealing, and it has deep roots. A hadith in Bukhari reports that Jibril went over the Qur'an with the Prophet ﷺ every Ramadan. The whole book, heard and said. Another hadith counts the reward by the letter: each letter a good deed, and each good deed multiplied by ten. And the one who stumbles is not left out. The Prophet said the skilled reciter is with the noble angels, and the one who struggles and stammers through it gets two rewards. So a family khatm, every voice in the room, Arabic understood or not, is honoring the whole book, every word of it. Now the case for slowing down. The Qur'an calls itself a blessed scripture sent so that people may ponder its verses, and asks those who won't: are there locks upon the hearts? When a young companion, Abdullah ibn Amr, wanted to finish faster and faster, the Prophet kept setting him a gentler pace, and would only let him go so far. Speed was never the goal. Here's what the two sides share, and it's worth telling a friend: neither wants a favorite corner. Both want the whole book, start to finish. One asks for every letter. The other asks for every meaning. A family can hold both: read it through together, and stop on one verse along the way.
screen: `THE CASE FOR FINISHING.` · `EVERY LETTER, EVERY STAMMER COUNTS.` · `THE CASE FOR SLOWING DOWN.` · `BOTH WANT ALL OF IT.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE BOOK.`

segments.voice: Read the Fatiha, in Arabic if you know it or in English if you don't, at your usual pace. Then read it once more at half the speed, listening to the sound of your own voice. Let one word you usually rush past stay with you until the time is up.
screen: `THE FATIHA, AT YOUR PACE.` · `AGAIN, AT HALF THE SPEED.` · `ONE WORD YOU USUALLY RUSH.`

segments.voice: The whole book: read through from beginning to end, letter by letter, meaning by meaning. A khatm seals it.
Hold onto this: a khatm honors every letter and every meaning, the whole book, not just the corner you love. Five of fifteen, and see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Muslims read the whole Qur'an through, a khatm, especially in Ramadan, sometimes alone and sometimes as a family or group, each person taking a part; others read slowly with a translation or commentary.

fork.setup: your study circle splits: half want to finish the whole Qur'an this Ramadan, half want one page a day with commentary. you're asked to give the 'finish it' side's best case. which is it?
options: Jibril went over the whole book with the Prophet each Ramadan, and every letter is rewarded.
finishing fast shows more devotion than understanding ever could.
the meaning is already settled, so there's nothing left to ponder.
fork.reveal: the strongest case for finishing rests on the Ramadan review with Jibril and the reward for each letter. the other side's case is just as real: the Qur'an asks to be pondered.

chat.says: dadi's planning a family khatm. cousin Sana called arabic we don't understand 'just sounds.' dadi's fuming. who's right?
options: Both have a point: stammering reciters are rewarded, and the book asks to be pondered.
Dadi. Only the Arabic sounds count; understanding was never part of it.
Sana. Without the meaning, reciting earns nothing, so it's a waste.
chat.meaning: The one who struggles through it gets two rewards (Muslim 798), and the Qur'an says it was sent to be pondered (38:29). Both views stand in the tradition.

tie.story: Jibril went over the whole Qur'an with the Prophet each Ramadan, and the Prophet kept slowing Abdullah ibn Amr down so he could take it in.

khatm.meaning: reading the whole Qur'an through; literally a sealing

Jibril.meaning: the angel Gabriel, who brought the Qur'an

Ramadan.meaning: the month of fasting, when the Qur'an is often read through

Abdullah ibn Amr.meaning: a young companion of the Prophet who wanted to read faster

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4998 (Jibril reviewed the Qur'an with the Prophet each Ramadan)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 2910 (each letter a good deed, multiplied by ten)

Sahih al-Bukhari 5052 (Abdullah ibn Amr and the pace of reading the whole Qur'an)
